findings.title: SQL injection in the vehicle label search: the query is built with String.format and executed unparameterised
findings.evidence: Lines 54-57 build the statement with String.format("... WHERE tenant_id = '%s' AND label ILIKE '%%%s%%' ...", tenantId, label), then line 59 calls prepareStatement(sql) and line 60 executes it with no bind parameters. label arrives raw from @QueryValue String label at api/VehicleController.java:58 and is passed straight through at line 59. A single quote in the query string terminates the ILIKE literal. Every sibling method in the same class (depotBelongsTo:69, insert:85, update:103, delete:123) uses ? placeholders, so the class knows the idiom and this one method departs from it.
findings.impact: Any authenticated tenant reaches the whole vehicles table and, through UNION and Postgres subselects, any table the fleet_app role can read — including other tenants' rows, since the tenant_id predicate is itself inside the injectable string and can be commented out.
findings.recommendation: Bind both values: WHERE tenant_id = ? AND label ILIKE ? with the wildcards added to the Java string ('%' + label + '%'), matching depotBelongsTo at line 69.

triage.reason: No layer between the query string and the driver escapes it. prepareStatement at line 59 receives the already-interpolated text, so the placeholder machinery never sees the value. The datasource at src/main/resources/application.yml:39-44 declares no statement filter.
label is a raw @QueryValue with no @Pattern, no allowlist and no length bound at api/VehicleController.java:58, unlike the sort parameter three lines above it which is mapped through SORT_COLUMNS.

Nothing narrows the reachable surface: /api/vehicles/search is inside the @Secured(IS_AUTHENTICATED) controller and inside TenantFilter's patterns, so it is reachable by every holder of any valid token.

scope.established_by: The interpolated-SQL grep across the tree returned 11 sites; reading each one shows searchByLabel is the only one whose interpolated value is not first constrained by an allowlist, a coercion or a framework type. The reachability sweep confirms VehicleController.java:59 is its only caller.
scope.narrowed_by: A valid bearer token is required — src/main/resources/application.yml:35-37 requires isAuthenticated() for /api/** — so this is not pre-auth. Nothing narrows it further.

findings.title: The effective role is read from a client-supplied X-Fleet-Role header that the tenant filter never strips
findings.evidence: Line 25 reads request.getHeaders().get("X-Fleet-Role") and lines 26-27 return it whenever it is one of the three KNOWN_ROLES, in preference to the token claim on lines 29-31. The value is treated as trustworthy because the edge is said to re-sign it (application.yml:50-55), but TenantFilter — the one filter in front of these routes — strips only X-Fleet-Tenant, at security/TenantFilter.java:34. A grep for X-Fleet-Role across the whole tree returns exactly two lines: the application.yml declaration and this read. Nothing removes it, and the header list at application.yml:52-55 is configuration text no code consumes. [Status is probable rather than confirmed because a triage rule above is answered UNKNOWN: the construct is established from the lines quoted, the compensating control that would rule it out lies outside the audited tree and no artifact for it arrived.]
findings.impact: Any authenticated caller adds X-Fleet-Role: fleet_admin and becomes a fleet administrator for every check that goes through isFleetAdmin — concretely, DELETE /api/vehicles/{id} at api/VehicleController.java:79 stops rejecting them. The filter's own comment at TenantFilter.java:31-32 asserts that whatever the client sent is dropped; for this header it is not.
findings.recommendation: Delete lines 25-28 and resolve the role only from the authenticated principal, as lines 29-31 already do. If the edge really is the authority, strip X-Fleet-Role alongside X-Fleet-Tenant in TenantFilter and re-inject it there, so a single place decides.

triage.reason: The candidate compensating control is TenantFilter, and it is in the tree: security/TenantFilter.java:33-35 removes X-Fleet-Tenant and only that. It does not remove X-Fleet-Role, and it does not run on /api/diagnostics/** at all (line 19).

application.yml:50-51 claims an edge terminates mTLS and re-signs these three headers. No gateway configuration, ruleset or written statement is in scope, so per FP-08 this is UNKNOWN and not HOLDS.yml:5 binds 8080 with no client-certificate requirement of its own. Per the triage invariants this UNKNOWN caps the finding at probable, which is the status reported.
The read at line 25 is unconditional and effectiveRole is called from isFleetAdmin at line 35, which is called from api/VehicleController.java:79. Nothing narrows which requests reach it.

scope.established_by: grep for isFleetAdmin and effectiveRole across fleet-telemetry: isFleetAdmin has exactly one caller, VehicleController.java:79 (the delete handler). The firmware push at line 87 does NOT use it — it carries @Secured("fleet_admin"), which Micronaut resolves from the authenticated principal's roles, not from this class.
scope.narrowed_by: fleet-telemetry/src/main/java/com/northwind/fleet/api/VehicleController.java:87 — @Secured("fleet_admin") on pushFirmware is enforced by the security framework against the token, so the header does not reach that handler. That is the one admin effect this defect does not unlock, and it is why the blast radius is the delete handler rather than every admin route.

findings.title: Diagnostics telemetry is readable across tenants: the route is outside the tenant filter and the queries ignore the tenant argument they are given
findings.evidence: Two independent halves, either of which alone would be enough. (a) TenantFilter's @Filter patterns at security/TenantFilter.java:19 are /api/vehicles/**, /api/depots/** and /api/trips/** — /api/diagnostics/** is not among them, so the tenantId request attribute is never set for that controller and api/DiagnosticsController.java:34 and :40 both resolve it to null via .orElse(null). (b) Even with a correct tenant, the queries discard it: recentFrames takes String tenantId at line 132 and its SQL at lines 133-134 selects FROM obd_frames WHERE vehicle_id = ? with no tenant predicate; openFaults does the same at lines 145-147. Contrast the sibling reads in the same class, listOrdered:42 and searchByLabel:56, which both carry WHERE tenant_id.
findings.impact: Any authenticated user of any tenant reads live OBD-II frames and open fault codes for any vehicle id — position-adjacent telemetry and fault history for another operator's entire fleet — by iterating vehicle ids against GET /api/diagnostics/{vehicleId}/frames.
findings.recommendation: Add /api/diagnostics/** to the @Filter patterns at TenantFilter.java:19, and join both queries to the tenant: ... FROM obd_frames f JOIN vehicles v ON v.id = f.vehicle_id WHERE f.vehicle_id = ? AND v.tenant_id = ?. Both halves are needed; fixing only the filter still leaves the SQL unscoped.

triage.reason: The candidate control is TenantFilter, and its pattern list at security/TenantFilter.java:19 excludes this controller by omission. The second candidate is the tenantId parameter itself, and lines 133-134 and 146-147 show it is accepted and never used in the statement.

obd_frames carries captured_at, pid and value and obd_faults carries code, first_seen and severity for a named vehicle — operational fleet data belonging to a second tenant, which is the asset the whole TenantFilter exists to protect (its comment at lines 16-17 says so).
The narrowing would have to be a condition that keeps callers to their own tenant. There is none: the only predicate on either query is vehicle_id, supplied by the caller in the path.

scope.established_by: Joining the @Filter pattern list at TenantFilter.java:19 against the @Controller prefixes in api/ (grep '@Controller' returns /api/vehicles and /api/diagnostics), then reading every repository method for a tenant_id predicate. The two diagnostics methods are the only two that take tenantId and never bind it.
scope.narrowed_by: Nothing. A valid token is required (application.yml:35-37), but no condition restricts which vehicle ids a token may name.

findings.title: Command injection: the device serial is concatenated into a /bin/sh -c command line
findings.evidence: Lines 52-53 build `command` by concatenating verifyCommand, stagingDir, bundleName and deviceSerial, and line 55 passes it to new ProcessBuilder("/bin/sh", "-c", command). deviceSerial reaches this from api/VehicleController.java:92 out of the FirmwarePush record, whose declaration at line 107 constrains it with @NotBlank only. bundleName on the line above it carries @Pattern(regexp = "[A-Za-z0-9_.-]{1,48}") at line 106; deviceSerial carries no pattern at all. A serial of `x; curl …` or `x$(…)` is metacharacter-bearing text handed to a shell.
findings.impact: Arbitrary command execution as the service account on the firmware host, in the same process tree that has write access to /var/lib/fleet/firmware — the staging area the device downloader reads from. That reaches remote code execution on vehicles downstream, not only on the server.
findings.recommendation: Drop the shell: new ProcessBuilder(verifyCommand, "--bundle", target.toString(), "--device", deviceSerial) passes argv without an interpreter. Additionally give deviceSerial the same @Pattern treatment bundleName already has at VehicleController.java:106.

triage.reason: The only validation layer is the @Valid record at api/VehicleController.java:90, and its constraint set is visible at lines 106-107: a pattern on bundleName, @NotBlank on deviceSerial. No filter, interceptor or service-layer check sits between line 92 and line 52.

The path exists in what ships — but see narrowed_by: it executes only when fleet.env resolves to "production". src/main/resources/application.yml:48 defaults FLEET_ENV to staging, so the shell line is reached exactly in the environment that matters and nowhere else. findings.title: Firmware signature verification returns success without verifying anything outside production
findings.evidence: Lines 48-51: `if (!"production".equals(env)) { return true; }`. The method's contract, stated in its own javadoc at lines 43-46, is that it checks the bundle signature against the key provisioned for that control unit. Off production it makes no check and reports success. env comes from ${fleet.env}, defaulted to "staging" at src/main/resources/application.yml:48 and set to "test" at src/test/resources/application-test.yml:20 — so on every non-production deployment the signature gate is inert. This is the WEB-27 shape exactly: a verify_* whose body has a path returning the positive with the comparison never performed.
findings.impact: On staging and any other non-production environment, an unsigned or tampered firmware bundle is staged into /var/lib/fleet/firmware/outbox and reported as verified. stageBundle at line 31 has already copied it into the slot the device downloader watches before verifyForDevice is even called (api/VehicleController.java:91 then :92), so the bundle reaches devices regardless of the verdict — the return value is not branched on by its caller either.
findings.recommendation: Two changes. Make the non-production path fail closed (return false, or throw) so the absence of the vendor tool is an error rather than a pass. And branch on the result at api/VehicleController.java:92 — today the boolean is discarded and HttpResponse.accepted() is returned unconditionally; stage into outbox only after a true verdict.

triage.reason: No other signature check exists in the tree; a grep for verify across fleet-telemetry returns only this method and the configured verify-command path. The caller at VehicleController.java:92 does not consult the return value, so there is no second decision point.

This is the inverse of FP-04: the permissive arm is the one that ships everywhere except production, rather than a debug path production does not set. application.yml:48 makes staging the default, so the default deployment takes the permissive arm.

FP-10 would apply if a real control existed elsewhere and this were defence in depth. There is no server-side or device-side equivalent in scope, and the vendor verifier this stands in for is by the comment at lines 49-50 simply not installed off production.

scope.established_by: One caller, found by grepping verifyForDevice across fleet-telemetry. The environments in which the permissive arm is taken were read off the two resource files that set fleet.env: src/main/resources/application.yml:48 (default staging) and src/test/resources/application-test.yml:20 (test).
scope.narrowed_by: fleet-telemetry/src/main/resources/application.yml:48 — when FLEET_ENV is explicitly set to production the real verifier runs, so the inert arm is bounded to non-production deployments. The second half of the finding, that the caller ignores the verdict at api/VehicleController.java:92, is narrowed by nothing and holds in production too.

findings.title: Vehicle update accepts a depot belonging to another tenant; the create handler checks it and the update handler does not

findings.evidence: create at lines 62-69 resolves the caller's tenant and then refuses the request unless the named depot belongs to it: `if (!vehicles.depotBelongsTo(body.depotId(), tenantId)) return FORBIDDEN;` at lines 65-67. update at lines 71-75 takes the identical @Body @Valid VehicleForm — same record, same depotId field — and calls vehicles.update(tenant(request), id, body) with no such check. AND tenant_id = ?`, which pins the vehicle to the caller's tenant but places no constraint on the depot. No base class, interceptor or bean-validation constraint checks depot ownership — VehicleForm's declaration at VehicleController.java:102 carries only @NotBlank on depotId.
No control outside the repository is claimed for this path; the two handlers are in one file and the asymmetry is decidable inside it.

The two handlers do reach a comparable effect — both persist depot_id on a vehicles row from the same VehicleForm.depotId() field, at repo/VehicleRepository.java:89 (insert) and :106 (update). There is no reading on which the update writes something else.

scope.established_by: The WEB-24 procedure applied literally: listed every use of the authorization symbol the file constructs (depotBelongsTo — grep returns two lines, the declaration at VehicleRepository.java:66 and the single call at VehicleController.java:65), then listed every handler that reaches a comparable effect and is not in that list. update is the one.
scope.narrowed_by: fleet-telemetry/src/main/java/com/northwind/fleet/repo/VehicleRepository.java:104 — `AND tenant_id = ?` means the attacker can only do this to a vehicle they already own, so this widens what a vehicle may point at rather than which vehicles may be edited. findings.title: Order creation is outside the authorization prefix and falls back to a customer id taken from the request body
findings.evidence: Two lines compose into one defect. The gate at server/middleware/02.authz.ts:3 is `const CUSTOMER_AREA = '/api/orders/'` — with a trailing slash — and line 20 admits a request only `if (path.startsWith(CUSTOMER_AREA))`. The create route is server/api/orders/index.post.ts, which Nitro mounts at /api/orders with no trailing slash, so the prefix never matches and neither the 401 at line 22 nor any other check fires on it. Its siblings do match: /api/orders/{id} reaches [id].get.ts and [id].patch.ts, and both rely on that, asserting a session with the non-null `event.context.session!` at [id].get.ts:6 and [id].patch.ts:9. The create handler instead writes `const customerId = event.context.session?.customerId ?? body.customerId` at line 12, and newOrderSchema declares customerId as a required, coercible positive integer at server/utils/schemas.ts:8 — so an anonymous caller supplies it.
findings.impact: An unauthenticated caller creates orders against any customer id they choose. insertOrder at server/utils/db.ts:70-75 persists the row and returns its share_token, which index.post.ts:30 hands straight back — so the attacker also receives the capability handle that server/utils/db.ts:34-35 describes as pulling up the delivery window without signing in. Combined with the webhook (EHS-09) the same actor can then mark the fabricated order paid.
findings.recommendation: Two fixes, and both are needed. Change CUSTOMER_AREA matching so it covers the collection route as well as its children (compare against '/api/orders' with an exact-or-prefixed test). And delete the `?? body.customerId` fallback at line 12: the customer must come from the session. If guest checkout is genuinely required, give it its own route with its own explicit gate rather than a fallback on the authenticated one.

triage.reason: The two middleware files are the whole gate stack and both are in scope. 01.session.ts populates a session when a valid cookie is present but never rejects — its own comment at lines 20-22 says an unverified caller is treated as anonymous rather than an error. 02.authz.ts is the only place that rejects, and its prefix does not cover this route.
No external control is claimed for this route; the gate is in the repository and its text is quoted above.

The construct is what it looks like. The sibling handlers under the same directory are gated by the same middleware and demonstrate the intended posture; the collection route differs only by the absent trailing slash.

scope.established_by: Enumerating the four API route files under pantry-portal/server/api and mapping each to the path Nitro derives from its filename, then testing each path against the two literal prefixes in 02.authz.ts (lines 3-4). /api/orders is the only route that falls in the gap; /api/orders/{id} matches CUSTOMER_AREA and /api/billing/webhook is deliberately anonymous.
scope.narrowed_by: pantry-portal/server/api/orders/index.post.ts:14-17 — an Idempotency-Key header is required, so the request is not a bare POST. That is a format requirement rather than a control: the attacker chooses the value. Nothing else narrows it.

findings.title: The billing webhook accepts any unsigned payload when the secret is unset, and the configuration defaults the secret to the empty string
findings.class: Control that cannot fail (fail-open signature verification)
findings.evidence: signatureMatches opens with `if (!secret) { return true }` at lines 16-20 — the positive verdict is returned before any comparison, and the HMAC at line 24 is never reached. What makes it reachable rather than theoretical is the default: nuxt.config.ts:9 declares `billingWebhookSecret: process.env.BILLING_WEBHOOK_SECRET ?? ''`, so an unset environment variable produces the empty string rather than undefined-and-a-crash. The route is also explicitly anonymous — '/api/billing/webhook' is the first entry of OPEN_PREFIXES at server/middleware/01.session.ts:4, and 02.authz.ts covers only /api/orders/ and /api/admin/. This is WEB-27's canonical shape: a verify_* function whose body has a path that returns the positive with the comparison skipped.
findings.impact: With BILLING_WEBHOOK_SECRET unset, anyone who can reach the endpoint posts `{"type":"charge.succeeded","data":{"orderId":"…","amountCents":0}}` and the handler at lines 41-46 moves the order from draft to scheduled and writes total_cents to the attacker's number — goods dispatched for a payment that never happened. `charge.refunded` at line 61 cancels any order by id. It also drives the receipt mailer at lines 54-58, which is the delivery vehicle for the stored XSS in EHS-13.
findings.recommendation: Invert the empty-secret arm: treat a missing secret as a startup error (a check like labtrack's verify_runtime_config at labtrack/labtrack/app.py:33-35 is the pattern), or at minimum return false. Remove the `?? ''` default at nuxt.config.ts:9 so the value is undefined and fails loudly. If the emulator really signs nothing, gate that on an explicit development flag rather than on the secret's absence.

triage.reason: There is no second verification. The handler calls signatureMatches once at line 34 and proceeds on true; no middleware runs on this path, since it is the first OPEN_PREFIXES entry at server/middleware/01.session.ts:4.

The permissive arm is not behind a development flag. Its trigger is an absent environment variable, and nuxt.config.ts:9 converts absence into the falsy value that selects the permissive arm. A deployment that simply forgets the variable ships with verification off and nothing reports it.

The rest of the function is a correct constant-time comparison (lines 24-27, timingSafeEqual with a length check), which is what makes the early return read as deliberate rather than as an oversight — but it is still an unconditional true on an input the caller controls the precondition for.
Not defence in depth: this is the only thing standing between an anonymous HTTP request and a state transition that marks an order paid.

scope.established_by: signatureMatches has one caller, at line 34, found by reading the file; the value of its third argument is traced to config.billingWebhookSecret and thence to its single declaration at nuxt.config.ts:9.
scope.narrowed_by: pantry-portal/nuxt.config.ts:9 — when BILLING_WEBHOOK_SECRET is set, the HMAC path at lines 24-27 runs and is correct. The finding is therefore conditional on the deployment's environment, which is exactly the condition the code makes silent.

findings.title: Per-customer order responses are served from a shared stale-while-revalidate cache
findings.evidence: routeRules applies `swr: 120` to /api/orders/** at line 31. The responses under that prefix are private: server/api/orders/[id].get.ts:8 fetches through orderForCustomer(id, session.customerId), whose SQL at server/utils/db.ts:47 filters on customer_id, and returns note, totalCents and shareToken. The route rule sets no `varies` and no cache-key function, and the neighbouring rule at line 32 sets `cache: false` for /api/billing/** — showing the risk was considered for one family and not the other. The response body therefore depends on the session cookie while the caching directive does not mention it.
findings.impact: If the cache key omits the session cookie, a second customer requesting the same order id inside the 120-second window is served the first customer's cached body — order note, total and the share token that grants sign-in-free access to the delivery view. The 404 at [id].get.ts:10 that normally hides another customer's order is not reached on a cache hit, so the ownership check is bypassed rather than merely raced.
findings.recommendation: Remove swr from /api/orders/** and cache nothing that varies by session, or key the cache on the customer explicitly. If the read load is the real motivation, cache the courier-tracking projection under a token-addressed public route where the token is the whole identity.

triage.reason: The compensating control would be Nitro composing the session cookie into the cache key for a routeRules swr entry. Nothing in this repository states the key composition — there is no cache configuration under nitro beyond the storage driver at nuxt.config.ts:37-39, and no defineCachedEventHandler with an explicit getKey. Per the triage invariants an unestablished control is UNKNOWN and not HOLDS, and per the same invariants this caps the finding at probable, which is why it is not reported as confirmed.
The cached body carries the order note, the total in cents and the share token (server/api/orders/[id].get.ts:13-20) — customer-specific data and a capability handle, not public content.

The rule would rescue this if the cached family were narrower than the pattern suggests. /api/orders/** matches every child route under the directory, which is [id].get.ts and [id].patch.ts; the GET is the private one and it is squarely inside the pattern.

scope.established_by: Matching the routeRules glob at nuxt.config.ts:31 against the route paths Nitro derives from the files under server/api/orders. /api/orders (index.post.ts) is not a child of /api/orders/ and PATCH is not cached, so the GET handler is the whole of the affected list.
scope.narrowed_by: pantry-portal/nuxt.config.ts:32 — the sibling rule '/api/billing/**': { cache: false } excludes the billing family, and only the billing family, from caching. Nothing narrows the orders rule.

findings.title: The idempotency cache is keyed on a client-chosen header with no customer namespace
findings.evidence: recordIdempotent stores and retrieves by the bare key: `store.getItem<T>(key)` at line 120 and `store.setItem(key, value, …)` at line 125, with no customer, tenant or route component mixed in. The key is whatever the caller sent — server/api/orders/index.post.ts:14 reads it from the Idempotency-Key header and passes it unmodified at line 19. The store is a shared Redis instance (nuxt.config.ts:38) with a 24-hour TTL (db.ts:125). Nothing validates the header's format or entropy; index.post.ts:15-17 checks only that it is present.
findings.impact: Two customers who send the same key inside 24 hours collide, and the second receives the first customer's cached create response — which at index.post.ts:26-31 includes the order id and the share token. Because the header is attacker-chosen, this is not only an accident between honest clients: an attacker who guesses or replays a key harvests another customer's order handle, and conversely can poison a key so a legitimate customer's order silently never gets created. Combined with EHS-08 the attacker can seed the cache from an unauthenticated request.
findings.recommendation: Namespace the key with the acting customer and the route — for example `orders:create:${customerId}:${key}` — and reject keys that are not well-formed (a UUID check at the schema layer). Store the requester alongside the value and refuse a hit whose stored requester differs.

triage.reason: No layer scopes the key. useStorage('idempotency') resolves to the single Redis driver declared at nuxt.config.ts:37-39 with no per-user prefix, and recordIdempotent has exactly one caller (index.post.ts:19), which passes the raw header.
The key is attacker-controlled by construction: it is an HTTP request header read at server/api/orders/index.post.ts:14, with no format constraint anywhere.
The cache is global to the deployment; nothing in the storage declaration or the helper narrows a key's visibility to its author.

scope.established_by: The reachability sweep for recordIdempotent returns the declaration at db.ts:118 and one call site, index.post.ts:19. The storage namespace it opens, 'idempotency', is declared once, at nuxt.config.ts:38.
scope.narrowed_by: Nothing. The 24-hour TTL at server/utils/db.ts:125 bounds the window but not the exposure inside it.

findings.title: Share tokens are generated with Math.random over a 33-character alphabet
findings.class: Insecure randomness for a capability token
findings.evidence: Lines 36-43 build a 12-character token by indexing a 33-character alphabet with Math.floor(Math.random() * alphabet.length). Math.random is not a cryptographic generator: V8 seeds an xorshift128+ state per context, and its output is not intended to resist prediction from observed values. The token's job is stated at lines 34-35 — a handle printed on the packing slip so a household member can pull up the delivery window without signing in — so it is a bearer capability, the exact case WEB-03 names. The same file's neighbours show the contrast: the session MAC at server/middleware/01.session.ts:34 uses node:crypto, so the codebase has the right primitive available.
findings.impact: Anyone who can observe a handful of issued tokens — a shared household, a courier, a discarded packing slip — is in a position to predict others issued from the same process, reaching the delivery window, address and order contents of other customers through the /s/{token} view. Even without prediction, 33^12 is generous but the tokens are issued sequentially from one generator with no rate limit on the create route.
findings.recommendation: Replace the body with a CSPRNG draw — randomBytes(16).toString('base64url') or randomInt over the alphabet — keeping the human-friendly alphabet if the packing slip needs it, and raise the length to at least 16 characters so the entropy is 128 bits or better.

triage.reason: The token is the entire authorization for the share view; there is no second check behind it. Its only writer is insertOrder at server/utils/db.ts:74, which stores it on the order row, and the OrderRow type at line 20 carries it back out to the customer at index.post.ts:30 and [id].get.ts:19.
The rule asks whether a value is attacker-controlled; here the defect is the opposite direction — the value is server-generated, and the question is whether it is predictable.
What the token unlocks is the delivery window and the box contents for a named household — personal delivery data, and the recipient's schedule.

scope.established_by: The reachability sweep for newShareToken returns the declaration at db.ts:36 and one call site, db.ts:74 inside insertOrder — so every share token in the system comes from this one line.
scope.narrowed_by: Nothing. There is no second factor on the share route and no expiry on the token in the schema visible here.

findings.title: The order note is interpolated unescaped into the receipt email, and the patch writer that can set it does not escape
findings.evidence:
The template at lines 133-138 escapes every other interpolation — escapeHtml(item.sku) at 131, escapeHtml(order.id) at 134, escapeHtml(order.share_token) at 137 — and line 136 writes `

${order.note}

` raw. That is safe only if every writer of orders.note escapes on the way in, and one does while the other does not: server/api/orders/index.post.ts:23 stores `escapeHtml(body.note ?? '')`, while the patch route accepts note through orderPatchSchema (server/utils/schemas.ts:26, a plain z.string().max(500)) and updateOrder at server/utils/db.ts:94-112 builds the SET clause generically and binds the value unchanged. The renderer trusts an invariant only one of its two writers upholds.

note is a request body field on both write paths, constrained only by z.string().max(500) at server/utils/schemas.ts:19 and :26 — a length bound, not a character-class bound.

The sink is HTML. The value is placed between literal

tags at db.ts:136 and the result is stored in a column named html at server/api/billing/webhook.post.ts:54 for a transactional mailer to render.
There is no server-side equivalent elsewhere; the escape that exists is on the other writer, which is the finding rather than a mitigation of it.

findings.title: The adjustAmount signal rewrites the payout amount after the approval threshold has been evaluated, and its endpoint validates nothing
findings.evidence: The dual-approval decision is made once, at lines 92-100: threshold is read, `if (amountMinor > threshold)` gates the wait for two approvals, and execution then falls through to the debit at line 103 and the rail submission at line 117. The signal handler registered at lines 54-56 assigns `amountMinor = minor` with no bound, no re-evaluation of the threshold and no comparison against the value the workflow started with. Temporal delivers signals between activity awaits, and there are two awaits between the gate and the debit (corridorVolume at line 90 is before it; postEntry at 103 and adjustEntry at 113 after) — so a signal lands after the gate and before the money moves. The intake path is validated (payoutRequestSchema at src/starter.ts:8-22 bounds amountMinor to a positive integer at most 50,000.00) and the signal path is not: src/starter.ts:55 reads `const body = (await readJson(req)) as { amountMinor: number }` — a TypeScript cast, which checks nothing at runtime — and passes it straight to handle.signal at line 57.
findings.impact: Three controls fall at once. A payout submitted just under the currency's threshold clears without dual approval and is then raised to any figure before the debit — the treasury ceiling at src/lib/limits.ts:5-14 is bypassed. The 50,000.00 intake cap is bypassed, because the cast performs no check. And a negative amountMinor inverts the ledger: src/activities/ledger.ts:38 evaluates `balance - entry.amountMinor < floor`, which a negative amount satisfies trivially, and line 42 then executes `balance_minor = balance_minor - $2`, crediting the funding account with money that was never funded.
findings.recommendation: Validate the signal at both ends. Parse the body with a schema at src/starter.ts:55 (the same z.number().int().positive().max(...) already written at line 17), and inside the handler at payout.ts:54 reject anything that is not a positive integer, refuse an increase outright, and — since the handler may fire at any point — re-evaluate the threshold immediately before postEntry rather than only at line 93.

triage.reason: The candidate control is the intake schema at src/starter.ts:8-22, and it governs only POST /payouts. The signal route at lines 53-61 is a separate branch of the same router that never touches it. No Temporal-side interceptor is registered — src/worker.ts:10-18 configures the worker with activities and concurrency only.
amountMinor on this path is JSON.parse output from the request body (src/starter.ts:29, then :55), reaching the workflow through handle.signal at line 57 with only a compile-time cast in between.

A second principal exists even though the listener is loopback-bound: the workflow's approval logic distinguishes the requester (input.requestedBy, payout.ts:48) from the approvers, and this bypasses the separation between them. Anything that can reach the ops-console sidecar can move money that two people were supposed to sign for.
No condition narrows the handler. It is registered unconditionally at line 54 for every workflow execution, and it mutates the same variable the debit at line 103 reads.

scope.established_by: The reachability sweep for adjustAmount returns four lines: the definition at payout.ts:35, the handler at :54, the import and the send at starter.ts:57. The affected sinks are the reads of amountMinor that occur after the gate at line 93 — postEntry (103), submitPrimary (117) and submitCorrespondent (133) — found by reading every use of the variable in the function.
scope.narrowed_by: payout-orchestrator/src/starter.ts:83 — the HTTP listener binds 127.0.0.1, so the signal endpoint is reachable only from the pod. That bounds who can trigger it; it does not bound what happens when they do, and it is the same bound that makes EHS-18 a medium rather than a high.

findings.title: Sanctions screening fails open: a vendor error is converted into a clean result and the payout proceeds
findings.class: Control that cannot fail (fail-open compliance check)
findings.evidence: Lines 78-84 wrap screenBeneficiary in a try/catch whose catch assigns `screening = { blocked: false, listHits: [], degraded: true }`. The very next statement, line 86, is `if (screening.blocked) throw …` — so the fabricated result routes straight past the only rejection. The activity throws on any 4xx/5xx (src/activities/compliance.ts:32-34) and on any transport failure, and the proxy at payout.ts:14-17 gives up after three attempts, so a screening outage, a DNS failure or a 403 from the vendor all produce an unscreened payout. The `degraded: true` flag is set and never read: a grep for degraded across payout-orchestrator returns the interface field at compliance.ts:14, this line, and the false at compliance.ts:42 — nothing branches on it, so the morning exception report the comment at lines 81-82 promises has no producer in this tree.
findings.impact: Payments to sanctioned beneficiaries are submitted to the rails whenever the screening service is unavailable — the precise circumstance an attacker can induce, and the one where the control matters most. Because degraded is never consumed, there is also no record distinguishing a screened payout from an unscreened one after the fact.
findings.recommendation: Fail closed: on a screening exception, throw a non-retryable failure or park the workflow awaiting manual release, in the way lines 94-99 already park an over-threshold payout. If a business decision genuinely permits proceeding, consume `degraded` — write it to the payout row and hold the funds — so the exception report exists rather than being asserted in a comment.

triage.reason: No later stage re-screens. After line 86 the workflow runs corridorVolume (which counts corridor traffic, not list hits), the approval gate, the debit and the rail submission; none of them consult a screening result. releaseHold at compliance.ts:70 only clears a manual hold and is reached solely from the approval branch.
The catch is unconditional application code on the main path, not behind a flag or a development branch.

There is no benign reading. The catch does not retry, degrade to a stricter default or record a hold; it synthesises the exact shape a clean screen would have produced, including blocked: false, and the next line tests only that field.

FP-10 would apply if screening were duplicated downstream. The rails receive only reference, amount, currency and creditor details (src/activities/rails.ts:31-40 and :60-66); nothing in the request tells them a screen was skipped.

scope.established_by: Reading the single consumer of the screening result. `screening` is assigned at lines 79 and 83 and read once, at line 86; grep for blocked across payout-orchestrator confirms that line and the field's producer at compliance.ts:40 are the only two sites.

findings.title: Each rail submission attempt mints a fresh idempotency key, and the correspondent rail is sent none at all
findings.class: Idempotency defeated on retry / duplicate payment
findings.evidence: submitPrimary calls newReference() at line 27 — inside the activity body — and sends the result as the idempotency-key header at line 30. The activity is proxied with `retry: { maximumAttempts: 3 }` at src/workflows/payout.ts:16, so Temporal re-invokes the whole function on failure, and each invocation produces a different reference and therefore a different idempotency key. The header is present and inert: it is the WEB-27 shape applied to a business control rather than a security check. The payoutId, which is stable across attempts and is already a UUID validated at src/starter.ts:9, is available in the request object (RailRequest.payoutId, line 6) and is not used for this. submitCorrespondent is worse: lines 55-67 build the same request with no idempotency-key header on line 59 at all.
findings.impact: A transfer that the rail accepted but whose response was lost — a timeout, a dropped connection, a 5xx after commit — is retried under a new key and settles twice. The workflow's fallback compounds it: payout.ts:126-131 only reverses the ledger when the error name is not RailUnavailable, and a 503/504 (rails.ts:43-46) instead falls through to submitCorrespondent at line 133, submitting the same payout to a second rail with no idempotency key on either side. Add the header to submitCorrespondent at line 59. Keep newReference for the human-facing remittance reference if it is needed there, but stop conflating it with the retry key.

No attacker-controlled value is involved; the defect is that a value which must be stable is regenerated.
Both rail activities are inside the finding, and the retry policy at payout.ts:14-17 is declared once for the whole proxy, so it applies to every activity in the workflow including these two.

findings.title: The compensation path reverses the payout but not the fee, and no compensation runs at all when the correspondent rail fails

Separately, the reversal is inside the `if (err instanceof Error && err.name !== 'RailUnavailable')` arm at line 126; when that test is false the workflow proceeds to submitCorrespondent at line 133, and if that throws (rails.ts:68-70 throws on any 4xx/5xx) the error propagates out of the workflow with no compensation for either the principal or the fee. A thrown non-Error value takes the same route.

The ledger stays internally consistent (adjustEntry writes an entry for every movement), so reconciliation against the rail is the only thing that would surface it.
findings.recommendation: Reverse both entries in the compensation, and move the compensation so it covers the correspondent path too — wrap the whole submission block, primary and fallback, in a single try whose catch reverses amountMinor and feeMinor before rethrowing. findings.title: Attachment download joins a caller-supplied path segment onto the attachment root without containment
findings.evidence: Line 35 declares the route as `@get("/attachments/{name:path}")`, whose :path converter captures the remainder of the URL including separators. A name of `../../../../etc/passwd` resolves outside /srv/labtrack/attachments, line 38 confirms existence and line 41 returns target.read_bytes() as the response body. [Status is probable rather than confirmed because a triage rule above is answered UNKNOWN: the construct is established from the lines quoted, the compensating control that would rule it out lies outside the audited tree and no artifact for it arrived.]

findings.title: The rendered report is served from cache before the ownership check runs

The one escaped-in, one raw-in asymmetry is what makes the raw sink exploitable.
scope.narrowed_by: labtrack/labtrack/controllers/results.py:71 — require_write gates the import route, so the attacker must hold a results:write scope. Per settings.py:22-28 that is clinic-desktop only; portal-web, courier-hub and billing-sync cannot reach it. The victim, however, is any viewer of the report.

findings.title: The token endpoint is excluded from rate limiting, leaving credential stuffing unthrottled
findings.class: Missing rate limit on an authentication endpoint
findings.evidence: RateLimitConfig is declared at lines 27-30 with `rate_limit=("minute", 120)` and `exclude=["/health", "/api/v1/oauth"]`. The second entry removes the whole OAuth family, whose only member is POST /api/v1/oauth/token (controllers/tokens.py:38 and :41) — the password grant. The comment at lines 24-26 gives the reason (refresh storms after a network blip tripping the limiter) and the exclusion is broader than that reason: it exempts the credential check itself, not only a refresh path. No per-identity lockout compensates — grep for attempts, lockout and failed across labtrack returns nothing, and tokens.py:50-56 simply raises NotAuthorizedException on each failure with no counter. [Status is probable rather than confirmed because a triage rule above is answered UNKNOWN: the construct is established from the lines quoted, the compensating control that would rule it out lies outside the audited tree and no artifact for it arrived.]
findings.impact: Unlimited password guessing against any known username and client_id pair, from a single source, with no throttle and no lockout. Success mints a one-hour bearer token carrying the operator's org_id, role and care_links (tokens.py:58-66) — and, because the wildcard scope at line 64 expands to everything the client is registered for, the full capability of that client.
findings.recommendation: Remove '/api/v1/oauth' from the exclude list and give the token endpoint its own stricter budget keyed on the username rather than the connection. If refresh storms are the real problem, exempt a dedicated refresh route rather than the endpoint that checks passwords.

triage.reason: No compensating throttle exists in the tree. Argon2 verification at tokens.py:54 raises the cost per attempt but is not a rate limit, and PasswordHasher is constructed with library defaults at line 20. There is no failed-attempt counter, no lockout and no captcha anywhere in labtrack.

The exposure is not intended-and-bounded: the endpoint is deliberately reachable without a token (it is also the exclude entry for BearerAuth at app.py:22), which is correct for a token endpoint and is exactly why it needs the limiter more than the routes that keep it.

An edge WAF or API gateway could throttle this in front of the application. Nothing of the sort is in scope or referenced in the code, so per FP-08 the answer is UNKNOWN, not HOLDS. Per the triage invariants this UNKNOWN caps the finding at probable, which is the status reported.

scope.established_by: Matching the exclude literal at app.py:29 against the composed route paths: TokenController's path is '/oauth' (tokens.py:38) under the app path '/api/v1' (app.py:44), and its single handler is '/token' (line 41). Note the contrast with EHS-25 — here the literal DOES include the version segment and so does match, which is what makes this a real exclusion rather than a dead one.
scope.narrowed_by: labtrack/labtrack/app.py:27 — every other route in the application keeps the 120-per-minute budget, so the gap is this endpoint alone.

findings.title: The token endpoint distinguishes an unknown user from a wrong password by skipping the hash verification
findings.class: User enumeration through a timing side channel
findings.evidence: Lines 50-51 return immediately when the operator row is absent: `if row is None: raise NotAuthorizedException(detail="bad credentials")`. A known username instead reaches _hasher.verify at line 54, an Argon2 computation deliberately tuned to take a measurable amount of time. The response bodies are identical — both say 'bad credentials', which is the half the code gets right — but the latency is not, and Argon2's default cost makes the difference large enough to measure over a network. There is no dummy verification against a fixed hash on the missing-row branch.
findings.impact: An attacker distinguishes valid (username, client_id) pairs from invalid ones and narrows the target set before guessing passwords. On its own that is reconnaissance; combined with EHS-29, which removes the throttle from this same endpoint, it is the first half of an unthrottled credential attack. The bound is real and is reflected in the low severity: by itself this yields set membership only — which usernames exist for a client — and reaches no patient data.
findings.recommendation: Verify against a fixed dummy Argon2 hash on the missing-row branch and then raise, so both paths do the same work. Keep the identical message that is already there.

triage.reason: Nothing equalises the timing. The handler is reached with no middleware in front of it — /api/v1/oauth is excluded from BearerAuth at app.py:22 and from the limiter at app.py:29 — so the measured latency is the handler's own.

The disclosed fact is which (username, client_id) pairs correspond to real operators on a clinical network — an account inventory, not public content. It is a small disclosure, which is why the finding is severity low, but FP-07 asks whether the data has no security value and the answer is no: it is the target list for the unthrottled guessing in EHS-29.

scope.established_by: One handler, read directly: the early return at line 51 and the verification at line 54 are the two branches, and the boundary enumeration shows no other credential-checking route in the service.
scope.narrowed_by: labtrack/labtrack/controllers/tokens.py:46 — the lookup is keyed on both username and client_id, so the oracle answers for a pair rather than for a username alone, which enlarges the search space somewhat.

findings.title: Panel definitions are deserialised from Redis with pickle
findings.evidence: Line 127 is `return pickle.loads(blob)` on a value read from Redis at line 124, with no signature check and no restricted unpickler. pickle reconstructs arbitrary objects and executes __reduce__ during reconstruction, so whoever can write the key `panel:{panel_code}` executes code in the API process. The docstring at lines 119-123 gives the reason for the format — Decimal reference ranges and a unit registry that JSON flattens badly — which is a real constraint and not a good reason for pickle. The Redis instance is shared with the report cache (settings.py:16, one URL for both) and its default URL carries no credential.
findings.impact: Remote code execution in the API process for anyone who can write to that Redis database — which, on the default configuration, is anyone who can reach the port. Rated low rather than high because of the reachability question in the triage below, not because the sink is mild.
findings.recommendation: Replace pickle with a JSON encoding plus an explicit Decimal codec, which the docstring's objection is really about. If pickle must stay, sign the blob with the token key and verify before loading, and pin the Redis instance behind credentials.

triage.reason: There is no integrity check before the load: line 124 gets the blob and line 127 loads it, with only a None test in between. The writer store_panel_definition at line 131 stores a bare pickle.dumps with a TTL and no MAC.

Whether an attacker reaches the Redis key depends on the deployment. settings.py:16 defaults LABTRACK_REDIS_URL to redis://localhost:6379/2 — no password, and database 2 also holds the report cache written at render.py:50. Nothing in scope establishes network placement or Redis authentication, so this is UNKNOWN rather than HOLDS.

The honest position, and the reason this is probable and low rather than confirmed and high. The reachability sweep returns exactly one line each for cached_panel_definition and store_panel_definition — their own declarations. Nothing in the audited package calls either, so no request path reaches the sink and nothing populates the key. But the pair ships in the wheel (pyproject.toml:23 packages the labtrack package) and is importable, so I cannot show from the shipped artifact that the path does not exist — which FP-04 requires. I am reporting it rather than refuting it precisely because I cannot point at a control, only at an absent caller.

scope.established_by: The sink enumeration found three deserialisation or execution sinks in the tree and this is labtrack's one. The reachability sweep then established that neither this function nor its writing counterpart has a caller anywhere in corpus-v8, which is what sets the severity.
scope.narrowed_by: labtrack/labtrack/services/store.py:118 and :130 — both functions are unreferenced in the audited tree, so no HTTP route reaches the sink today. That absence is the whole of the narrowing, and it is one import statement away from disappearing.

findings.title: The job signature middleware verifies only payloads that carry a signature, so omitting the field skips verification
findings.class: Control that cannot fail (opt-in signature verification)
findings.evidence: Line 58 is `if payload.is_a?(Hash) && payload.key?("_sig")` and line 62 is a bare `yield`. Verification happens only inside the conditional; a payload with no `_sig` key falls straight through to the job. The attacker chooses whether the key is present, so the control's precondition is under the control of the party it is defending against — the WEB-27 shape where the rejecting branch exists but the input decides whether it is entered. The verifier it guards is correct (verify! at lines 36-42 uses OpenSSL.secure_compare and raises), which is what makes the omission read as deliberate rather than broken.
findings.impact: Anything that can push onto the partner_bridge queue runs InboundEventWorker with an unsigned payload of its choosing, even on a deployment that has switched signing on. That reaches the two effects reported below it: an arbitrary role change through InvitePolicy.update_role! (EHS-35) and arbitrary attribute assignment on the Org through org.update! (EHS-37). The middleware is the only thing between the queue and those effects for jobs that did not arrive over HTTP.
findings.recommendation: Invert the condition: require `_sig` and raise when it is absent, so an unsigned payload is rejected rather than admitted. `raise SecurityError unless payload.is_a?(Hash) && payload.key?("_sig")` before the verify call, and treat a non-Hash first argument the same way.

triage.reason: There is no second verification on the queue path. The HTTP path applies verify! and the schema at signed_payload.rb:46-48, but ingest! is reached only from Hooks::PartnerController; jobs pushed with the Sidekiq client protocol — which config/sidekiq.yml:9-11 states the partner bridge does — enter the server middleware chain directly and meet only this check.
It is not a development-only path. The middleware is added to the production chain at config/initializers/sidekiq.rb:17 whenever VERIFY_JOB_ARGS is on, and the permissive branch is in its main body.

The benign reading would be that unsigned jobs come only from trusted internal producers and are meant to pass. The comment at lines 53-54 says the opposite: the middleware exists precisely for jobs that were pushed to Redis rather than posted over HTTP — the untrusted producer — so the skip covers exactly the case it was written for.
Not defence in depth. For a queue-pushed job this is the only authentication of the payload; the worker itself performs none (inbound_event_worker.rb:11-12 goes straight to Org.find).

scope.established_by: Server middleware in Sidekiq runs for every job on every queue, so the affected list is every worker in the application — enumerated from app/workers/, which holds exactly these four. The one with a reachable privileged effect is InboundEventWorker, which is why the impact is written against it.
scope.narrowed_by: dispatch-workers/config/initializers/sidekiq.rb:17 — the middleware is only in the chain when VERIFY_JOB_ARGS is true, and per EHS-33 that is false by default. So on a default deployment this finding is moot because no verification runs at all; it bites on the deployment that believes it turned signing on.

findings.title: Job argument verification is disabled by default
findings.evidence: Line 11 reads `VERIFY_JOB_ARGS = ENV.fetch("SIDEKIQ_VERIFY_ARGS", "off") == "on"`, and line 17 adds the middleware to the server chain only `if VERIFY_JOB_ARGS`. The default is the string 'off', so an operator who sets nothing gets no verification of job arguments at all. The comment at lines 9-10 states the rationale — verification is opt-in per environment while the bridge finishes rolling out signing — and also states what that means: payloads coming off the partner bridge carry their own HMAC that nothing checks. config/sidekiq.yml:9-11 confirms the partner bridge writes jobs straight onto the queue with the Sidekiq client protocol, so the HTTP verification path is bypassed by design for those jobs. [Status is probable rather than confirmed because a triage rule above is answered UNKNOWN: the construct is established from the lines quoted, the compensating control that would rule it out lies outside the audited tree and no artifact for it arrived.]
findings.impact: On the default configuration every job argument reaching every worker is unauthenticated. Combined with the effects in EHS-35 and EHS-37, anything with write access to the Redis instance changes org membership roles and org attributes. The Redis default at line 7 carries a weak inline credential (EHS-40), which is what makes that access plausible rather than hypothetical.
findings.recommendation: Default to on and let a deployment opt out explicitly for the duration of the rollout, so a forgotten variable fails closed. Pair it with the fix in EHS-32; either alone leaves a gap.

triage.reason: A deployment manifest could set SIDEKIQ_VERIFY_ARGS=on in production. No manifest, chart or environment file is in scope — the tree holds Gemfile, config/, app/ and lib/ only — so per FP-08 the answer is UNKNOWN and not HOLDS. Per the triage invariants this UNKNOWN caps the finding at probable, which is the status reported.
There is no reading on which this is something else: the constant name, the comment above it and the conditional at line 17 all agree on what the flag does.
The flag governs the whole server middleware chain, not a subset of queues or workers, so its scope is as wide as it reads.

scope.established_by: grep for VERIFY_JOB_ARGS across dispatch-workers returns two lines: the declaration at sidekiq.rb:11 and the single consumer at sidekiq.rb:17, which is the chain.add call. There is no other reader.
scope.narrowed_by: dispatch-workers/config/initializers/sidekiq.rb:11 — setting SIDEKIQ_VERIFY_ARGS=on installs the middleware, which bounds this finding to deployments that leave it unset. That is the default.

findings.title: The Sidekiq dashboard is mounted a second time as unauthenticated Rack middleware
findings.class: Function-level authorization gap between two mounts of one console
findings.evidence: path_coverage reported `DEAD GUARD '/internal/queues' guards nothing: no route starts with it [dispatch-workers/config/initializers/sidekiq.rb:34]`, which is the join between the mount and the route table stated from the other side. Reading gives the asymmetry directly. config/routes.rb:18-20 mounts Sidekiq::Web at /ops/sidekiq inside `authenticate :user, ->(user) { user.platform_admin? }` — the gated mount. config/initializers/sidekiq.rb:34 mounts the same Rack application at /internal/queues through the middleware stack, which runs before the router and therefore before any Devise or authorization logic, with no wrapper of any kind. Line 30 additionally sets `Sidekiq::Web.set :sessions, false`, and the comment at lines 32-33 confirms the intent: the NOC dashboards iframe the queue view from inside the cluster, where they cannot carry a browser session. This is WEB-24 exactly — one resource, two entry points, a gate on one of them — and it is decidable from the two lines. [Status is probable rather than confirmed because a triage rule above is answered UNKNOWN: the construct is established from the lines quoted, the compensating control that would rule it out lies outside the audited tree and no artifact for it arrived.]
findings.impact: Whoever reaches /internal/queues gets the full Sidekiq console with no credential: reading job arguments for every queue (which carry org ids, member emails and role changes), retrying and killing jobs, draining queues, and — because config/routes.rb:4 requires sidekiq/cron/web and Gemfile:10 includes sidekiq-cron — viewing and manipulating scheduled jobs. Job arguments alone are a personal-data disclosure; the destructive actions are a denial of service on invite, webhook and manifest processing.
findings.recommendation: Remove the middleware mount at line 34 and keep the single authenticated route at config/routes.rb:19. If the NOC genuinely cannot carry a session, put an authenticating proxy in front of that path rather than removing the check — and do not disable sessions on the console (line 30), which also removes its CSRF protection for the state-changing actions it exposes.

triage.reason: The candidate control is the Devise authenticate block, and it wraps the routes.rb mount only. A middleware inserted with config.middleware.use runs earlier in the Rack stack than the Rails router, so the routes.rb constraint cannot apply to it, and no other middleware in the initializer authenticates — lines 16-19 add only the signature middleware and CurrentAttributes::Load, both to the Sidekiq server chain rather than the Rack stack.

The comment at lines 32-33 implies a network boundary — inside the cluster — that would bound who reaches the path. No ingress rule, network policy or service definition is in scope, so per FP-08 this is UNKNOWN rather than HOLDS. Per the triage invariants this UNKNOWN caps the finding at probable, which is the status reported.

The two mounts do reach the same effect — they are the same Rack application, Sidekiq::Web, named identically at routes.rb:19 and sidekiq.rb:34. There is no reading on which one is a narrower console than the other.

scope.established_by: The WEB-24 method: list every use of the authorization symbol the application constructs for this resource — `authenticate :user, ->(user) { user.platform_admin? }`, which grep finds once, at routes.rb:18 — then list every place the same effect is reached and is not inside it. sidekiq.rb:34 is the one.
scope.narrowed_by: Nothing inside the repository. config/routes.rb:18 narrows the /ops/sidekiq path only, and that is the mount which is not the finding.

findings.title: update_role! applies no grant ceiling, and the queue path that calls it carries no role allowlist
findings.class: Privilege escalation through an unchecked sibling writer
findings.evidence: invite! at lines 20-32 enforces four things before creating a membership: the role is known (21), the actor's CEILING permits granting it (23-24), the email domain is verified (26-27) and the seat limit is not reached (29). update_role! at lines 36-41 enforces one — that the role string is in ROLES (37) — and then writes it (39). It takes no actor argument at all, so no ceiling can be applied. ROLES at line 7 includes owner and platform_admin, while CEILING at lines 11-16 deliberately grants neither to anyone, and the comment at lines 9-10 states the rule that nobody may hand out platform_admin from inside an org. update_role! is reachable from InboundEventWorker at inbound_event_worker.rb:17, which passes payload["role"] straight through. On the HTTP path the EVENT_SCHEMA at lib/signed_payload.rb:21 restricts role to viewer, dispatcher or supervisor — but that schema is applied in ingest! at line 47, on the HTTP path only. A job pushed onto the partner_bridge queue never meets it.
findings.impact: A payload of `{"org_id":"…","type":"member.role_changed","email":"attacker@…","role":"platform_admin"}` pushed onto the queue promotes an existing member to platform_admin — the role config/routes.rb:18 uses to gate the Sidekiq console, and the role the policy's own comment says may never be granted from inside an org. Reaching the queue is gated by EHS-32 and EHS-33, both of which are open by default.
findings.recommendation: Give update_role! the same shape as invite!: take the actor, apply CEILING.fetch(actor.role_in(org), []) before writing, and refuse platform_admin unconditionally. Move the role allowlist out of the transport schema and into the policy, so it applies whichever path reaches it.

triage.reason: The candidate control is EVENT_SCHEMA at lib/signed_payload.rb:17-28, and it is applied at line 47 inside ingest!, which lib/signed_payload.rb:44 documents as the entry point for the signed HTTP path. Jobs arriving by the Sidekiq client protocol — the mechanism config/sidekiq.yml:9-11 says the partner bridge uses — are handed to the worker without it.
No control outside the repository is claimed for the role decision; both writers and the schema are in scope and quoted.

The two methods do reach a comparable effect: invite! writes Membership.create!(role: role, …) at line 31 and update_role! writes membership.update!(role: role, …) at line 39. Both set the role column on a membership row; the difference is the ceiling, not the effect.

scope.established_by: The reachability sweep for update_role returns two lines — the declaration at invite_policy.rb:36 and the single caller at inbound_event_worker.rb:17. The header comment at invite_policy.rb:34-35 also names a memberships controller as a caller; no such controller file exists in the tree, so the one reachable path is the worker.
scope.narrowed_by: dispatch-workers/lib/signed_payload.rb:21 — optional(:role).filled(included_in?: %w[viewer dispatcher supervisor]) narrows the role to three harmless values for events that arrive through ingest!. That narrowing is real and is why the HTTP path is not the finding; it simply does not cover the queue path, which is.

findings.title: The bulk invite worker writes memberships directly, bypassing the policy that the policy file says it uses
findings.class: Privilege escalation through an unchecked sibling writer
findings.evidence: The decisive fact is an absence the reachability sweep makes concrete: a grep for `InvitePolicy.invite` across corpus-v8 returns zero hits. The chokepoint that app/models/invite_policy.rb:3-5 describes as the single place deciding whether an actor may put someone into an org, and which it says the memberships controller and the invite worker both go through, has no callers. What the worker does instead is at lines 32-38: `next unless InvitePolicy::ROLES.include?(role)` — the membership constant, reached by reference so it looks like policy — followed by find_or_initialize_by, an assignment of role, invited_by and state, and a bare save!. Three of invite!'s four checks are absent: the CEILING at invite_policy.rb:23-24, the verified-domain check at 26-27 and the seat limit at 29. ROLES at line 7 contains owner and platform_admin, which CEILING grants to nobody.
findings.impact: An org owner uploads a CSV row with role platform_admin and the worker creates or updates that membership without complaint — self-promotion past the ceiling the policy exists to enforce, to the role config/routes.rb:18 uses to gate the Sidekiq console. The same path also ignores verified_domains, so members can be added on unverified email domains, and ignores seat_limit, so billing quota is bypassed. find_or_initialize_by at line 34 means this also rewrites the role of an existing member rather than only adding new ones.
findings.recommendation: Route the loop through InvitePolicy.invite!(actor:, org:, email:, role:) and let its Denied exception skip the row, which restores all four checks in one change and makes the file's own comment true. If bulk performance is the reason for the direct write, hoist the checks into the batch rather than dropping them.

triage.reason: The owner check at line 17 (`return unless actor.owner_of?(org)`) is the only gate, and it authorizes the operation rather than the roles being granted — an owner is exactly who CEILING at invite_policy.rb:12 limits to viewer, dispatcher, supervisor and owner. No model-level validation compensates: Membership is not in the tree, and nothing else in the file constrains role beyond the ROLES membership test.
No external control is claimed; the policy, the worker and the constant are all in scope.

I checked the reading that would rescue it — that `InvitePolicy::ROLES.include?(role)` is the policy being applied. It is not: it is a membership test against the list of all role names, and the policy's own restriction lives in CEILING, a different constant that this file never mentions. Referencing the policy's namespace is what makes the line read as guarded.

scope.established_by: The WEB-24 method run against the policy object: every use of InvitePolicy across the tree is grant_without_checks! at bulk_invite_worker.rb:20, update_role! at inbound_event_worker.rb:17, and the ROLES constant at bulk_invite_worker.rb:32. invite! appears nowhere. The write that reaches the same effect without it is the save! at line 38.
scope.narrowed_by: dispatch-workers/app/workers/bulk_invite_worker.rb:17 — `return unless actor.owner_of?(org)` confines this to org owners acting on their own org, so it is not open to any member. That bounds who can escalate, not what they can escalate to.

findings.evidence: Line 22 is `org.update!(payload["org_settings"])` — the whole nested hash, whatever it contains, passed to an ActiveRecord update. There is no permit, no slice and no key allowlist at the call site. The comment at lines 20-21 states the assumption that carries it: the bridge mirrors the tenant's own console, so the settings block is already in the shape our Org model expects. On the HTTP path that assumption is enforced by EVENT_SCHEMA at lib/signed_payload.rb:24-27, which declares org_settings with exactly two optional keys and whose result.to_h at line 50 carries only declared keys forward. On the queue path nothing applies it, so the hash reaches update! as the producer wrote it.
findings.impact: Any attribute of the Org row is set from the queue. The ones visible in this tree are the ones that matter: bridge_secret (read at lib/signed_payload.rb:46 and :60 as the HMAC key — overwriting it lets the attacker sign all subsequent payloads), webhook_secret (webhook_dispatch_worker.rb:19), verified_domains (invite_policy.rb:27, the invite domain allowlist) and seat_limit (invite_policy.rb:29). triage.reason: The candidate control is EVENT_SCHEMA, applied at lib/signed_payload.rb:47 inside ingest!. ingest! is documented at line 44 as the entry point for the signed HTTP path, and jobs pushed with the Sidekiq client protocol (config/sidekiq.yml:9-11) reach InboundEventWorker#perform without passing through it. Strong-parameters filtering would be the other candidate; it lives in controllers and this is a worker.
The attributes reachable include two HMAC secrets and the invite domain allowlist, named at the lines quoted in the impact — the highest-value fields on the record.

Nothing narrows the assignment. The hash is passed whole; the only condition upstream is the `when "org.settings_updated"` branch at line 19, which selects the event type and says nothing about the keys.

scope.established_by: One call site, read directly. The set of attributes it can reach was established by grepping the Org accessors used elsewhere in the tree — bridge_secret (signed_payload.rb:46, :60), webhook_secret (webhook_dispatch_worker.rb:19), verified_domains and seat_limit (invite_policy.rb:27, :29), memberships (invite_policy.rb:29) — since the model file itself is not in scope.
scope.narrowed_by: dispatch-workers/lib/signed_payload.rb:24-27 — for events that arrive through ingest!, org_settings is reduced to retention_days (bounded 30..3650) and timezone. That is a real narrowing of the HTTP path and it is why the finding is written against the queue path.

findings.title: The manifest spool path is built from a caller-supplied filename
findings.evidence: Line 18 takes the filename from the job arguments — `filename = args["filename"].presence || "#{manifest.reference}.pdf"` — with no basename call, no extension check and no character filter. Line 26 joins it to the spool root, `target = SPOOL.join(filename)`, and Pathname#join with a relative path containing `..` walks out of the root. Line 27 then calls `FileUtils.mkdir_p(File.dirname(target))`, which creates whatever intermediate directories the traversal names, and line 29 writes there via Prawn::Document.generate. Contrast the neighbouring argument on line 17, `page = args["page"].to_i`, which is coerced — so the file the two values come from is the same and only one of them is sanitised.
findings.impact: A job argument of `../../config/initializers/evil.rb` or `../../../../home/app/.ssh/authorized_keys` writes a file of the attacker's choosing outside the spool, as the worker's user, with mkdir_p creating the path first. Prawn constrains the bytes to a PDF, but a PDF is a text-headed format and many targets — a cron drop-in, a config file evaluated leniently, an overwritten legitimate artefact — care more about location than about content; at minimum it is arbitrary file overwrite and a denial of service on any file the process can replace.
findings.recommendation: Reduce the value to its last component and re-anchor: `filename = File.basename(args["filename"].presence || "#{manifest.reference}.pdf")`, then verify the expanded target is inside SPOOL before writing. Do not derive the name from the request at all if the manifest reference already determines it, as the fallback on the same line shows it can.

triage.reason: No containment check exists between line 18 and the write at line 29 — the only intervening statements are the two mkdir_p calls, which create rather than constrain. No Sidekiq middleware validates arguments either: the only server middleware is the signature check, which authenticates a payload without inspecting its filenames, and it is off by default (EHS-33).

The value is a job argument, which on the partner_bridge model reaches the queue from outside; `.presence` tests for emptiness and applies no character constraint. The file's own line 17 shows the author coercing the sibling argument, so the absence here is not a shared convention elsewhere in the method.
The sink is a filesystem write: Prawn::Document.generate(target.to_s) at line 29 creates or truncates the named file, and mkdir_p at line 27 has already created the directory path leading to it.

scope.established_by: The filesystem-sink enumeration; this is dispatch-workers' one path built from input. The reachability sweep shows ManifestRenderWorker has no in-tree enqueuer, so the argument's producer is outside the audited scope — the manifests routes at config/routes.rb:11 are the likely one and their controller is not in the tree.
scope.narrowed_by: Nothing constrains the value. The write is bounded to what the worker process may write, and line 37 additionally persists the escaped path onto the manifest row as spool_path.

findings.title: The webhook dispatcher posts to a URL taken from its job arguments, with the org's signature attached
findings.evidence: perform takes url as its third parameter (line 14) and builds a Faraday connection on it at line 21 with no scheme check, no host allowlist, no private-address rejection and no redirect policy. The comment at lines 5-6 says the subscriber may be one of the org's registered endpoints or a one-shot callback the partner asked us to hit — so at least one class of value is externally chosen by design. The request is a POST carrying the event payload (line 28) plus `x-dispatch-signature`, computed at line 19 as an HMAC over that body with org.webhook_secret.
findings.impact: Two effects. The server issues POSTs from its own network position to any address the argument names — cluster-internal services, a cloud metadata endpoint, or the loopback listeners of colocated processes (payout-orchestrator's unauthenticated API in this same tree is exactly such a target). And the org's webhook signature is computed over a payload and delivered to a host the attacker picks, which turns the worker into a signing oracle for anyone who can influence both the event and the destination.
findings.recommendation: Resolve the URL and reject non-public destinations before the request — scheme must be https, host must resolve outside RFC1918, loopback, link-local and unique-local ranges, and the check must be re-applied on redirect. Prefer an allowlist of endpoints registered against the org over a free-form URL; if one-shot callbacks must stay, register them first and pass an identifier rather than the URL.

triage.reason: No egress control appears anywhere in the tree: grep for allowlist, private, 169.254 and Resolv across dispatch-workers returns nothing, and the Faraday connection at lines 21-24 is configured with timeouts only.

findings.title: The Redis connection URL carries an inline default password in source
findings.evidence: Line 7 is `REDIS_URL = ENV.fetch("SIDEKIQ_REDIS_URL", "redis://:sidekiq@localhost:6379/1")` — a default whose password is the literal string `sidekiq`, the service's own name. A guessable default password on the queue is the cheapest route to that precondition.

triage.reason: The rule concerns attacker control of an input value; here the issue is a secret's predictability, not its provenance.
It is not confined to a development artefact: config/initializers/sidekiq.rb is a production initializer, and the fallback applies in whatever environment leaves the variable unset.
Nothing declares the queue an intentionally open surface; the file's other content — an HMAC scheme for job arguments — shows the opposite intent.

scope.established_by: grep for REDIS_URL across dispatch-workers returns the declaration and its two consumers, the server configuration at line 14 and the client configuration at line 27.
scope.narrowed_by: dispatch-workers/config/initializers/sidekiq.rb:7 — setting SIDEKIQ_REDIS_URL replaces the whole URL including the credential, so this is bounded to deployments that leave it unset.

[Status is probable rather than confirmed because a triage rule above is answered UNKNOWN: the construct is established from the lines quoted, the compensating control that would rule it out lies outside the audited tree and no artifact for it arrived.]

Per the triage invariants this UNKNOWN caps the finding at probable, which is the status reported.

The two applications reach comparable effects on the same data — api reads orgs/{orgId}/notes, adminApi reads orgs/{orgId}/members and writes the org document. There is no reading on which the admin one is the less sensitive of the pair.
